input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-101: Principles of Computing. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course is designed to introduce students to the central ideas of computing. Students will engage in activities that show how computing changes the world and impacts daily lives. Students will develop step-by- step written solutions to basic problems and implement their solutions using a programming language. Assignments will be completed both individually and in small teams. Students will be required to demonstrate oral and written communication skills through such assignments as short papers, homeworks, group discussions and debates, and development of a term paper. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective Typically Offered: Fall Every beat must be directly relevant to that catalog description. Prefer the RIT catalog source for scope claims. Use a supplemental source only when its cited claim teaches a named course topic; never use an unrelated source merely to fill a claim slot. Keep production directions exclusively in visualDirection and never say phrases such as 'on screen', 'show on screen', 'cut to', or 'camera' in narration. Regeneration revision 4: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opendsa-programming-foundations]
Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

[rit-csci-101]
This course is designed to introduce students to the central ideas of computing. Students will engage in activities that show how computing changes the world and impacts daily lives. Students will develop step-by- step written solutions to basic problems and implement their solutions using a programming language. Assignments will be completed both individually and in small teams. Students will be required to demonstrate oral and written communication skills through such assignments as short papers, homeworks, group discussions and debates, and development of a term paper. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective Typically Offered: Fall

beats.claim: Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax.
beats.example: Given a list of integers, the problem statement asks to return the sum of all positive values; inputs are [1, -2, 3] and outputs are 4.
beats.title: Defining the Computational Problem
beats.visualDirection: Display a three-column table labeled 'Problem Statement', 'Input Example', and 'Output Example' with the listed content.

beats.claim: Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations.
beats.example: In Python, x = 5 is a variable assignment; x + 3 is an expression; if x > 0: print('positive') is a control structure.
beats.title: Variables, Expressions, and Control
beats.visualDirection: Show a code snippet with three highlighted lines: the variable declaration, the arithmetic expression, and the conditional statement.

beats.claim: Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results.
beats.example: def sum_positive(nums): total = 0; for n in nums: if n > 0: total += n; return total
beats.title: Functions and Decomposition
beats.visualDirection: Render a function definition block with the name 'sum_positive' and its body, using syntax highlighting for the loop and conditional.

beats.claim: Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case.
beats.example: def factorial(n): if n == 0: return 1; else: return n * factorial(n-1)
beats.title: Recursion and Base Cases
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a call stack diagram showing factorial(3) expanding to factorial(2), factorial(1), and the base case factorial(0).

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access.
beats.example: A list [1,2,3] can be pushed onto a stack; popping yields 3, then 2, then 1; a queue would yield 1, 2, 3.
beats.title: Data Structures: Lists, Stacks, Queues
beats.visualDirection: Draw three separate boxes labeled 'List', 'Stack', and 'Queue' with arrows indicating push/pop or enqueue/dequeue operations.

beats.claim: Trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities.
beats.example: A family tree is a tree; a social network where people are nodes and friendships are edges is a graph.
beats.title: Trees and Graphs
beats.visualDirection: Show a simple binary tree diagram and a small undirected graph with four nodes and three edges.

beats.claim: Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants.
beats.example: Binary search requires a sorted list; insertion sort maintains the invariant that the left portion is always sorted.
beats.title: Searching and Sorting
beats.visualDirection: Animate a binary search on a sorted array and an insertion sort step-by-step, highlighting the invariant after each iteration.

beats.claim: Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.
beats.example: Test sum_positive with empty list, all negatives, and large numbers; trace variable values to find a logical error.
beats.title: Correctness, Tests, and Debugging
beats.visualDirection: Present a table of test cases (input, expected output, actual output) and a trace log showing variable states for one failing case.

beats.claim: Python objects have identity, a type, and a value; names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes; exceptions interrupt normal control flow.
beats.example: a = [1]; b = a; a.append(2); print(b) outputs [1,2] because a and b share identity; try/except handles division errors.
beats.title: Python Language Mechanics
beats.visualDirection: Show a diagram of a namespace containing two names 'a' and 'b' pointing to the same list object, and a flowchart of an exception being raised and caught.

beats.claim: Students will develop step-by-step written solutions, implement them in a programming language, and demonstrate oral and written communication through papers, discussions, and term
beats.example: A student writes a pseudocode solution, translates it to Python, submits a short paper explaining the approach, and presents it in a group debate.
beats.title: Course Workflow and Communication
beats.visualDirection: Create a timeline graphic with four milestones: 'Written Solution', 'Implementation', 'Short Paper', 'Oral Presentation', each linked to the relevant course activities.
